narrative:
**EOD Macro-Risk Brief | 2026-09-24**

**Headline:**
Systemic risk remains High, driven by opaque leverage in credit markets and geopolitical supply-chain weaponization.

**Key Stories (No Changes Today):**
• **Private credit's opaque expansion** (High): Unregulated balance-sheet growth and maturity mismatches create contagion risk if redemptions accelerate.
• **Sea lanes & undersea cables** (High): Geopolitical fragility threatens critical infrastructure; disruption would cascade through trade and data flows.
• **Japan fiscal / JGB / carry trade** (High): Structural imbalances and yen volatility expose leveraged positions to rapid unwinding.
• **Critical minerals as a weapon** (High): Supply concentration in geopolitically hostile regions creates industrial and energy-transition bottlenecks.
• **Treasury basis trade** (Elevated): Hidden leverage in repos and derivatives increases rollover risk in stress scenarios.
• Nine additional Elevated-level risks span emerging-market debt, China deflation, CRE, eurozone fragility, AI financing, and commodity constraints.

**Watch Most Closely:**
Private credit's opaque expansion poses the highest systemic trigger—opacity prevents early detection of stress.

stories.name: Treasury basis trade (hidden leverage)

indicators.label: SOFR minus EFFR (%)
MOVE index (Treasury volatility)
SEC central clearing on track (0 ok / 1 slipping / 2 delayed)

stories.summary: Hedge funds run a highly leveraged arbitrage between Treasury cash bonds and futures. It is a major source of liquidity, but a spike in funding costs or Treasury volatility can force rapid unwinds, as briefly happened in March 2020 and again in 2025.

stories.name: Japan fiscal / JGB / carry trade

indicators.label: USD/JPY (yen strengthening = lower = risk)
30-year JGB yield (%)
Takaichi plan financing clarity (0 ok / 1 unclear / 2 disorderly)

stories.summary: Decades of near-zero rates made Japan the funding leg of a vast global carry trade. As the BoJ normalizes and JGB yields rise, fiscal financing gets harder and carry unwinds can transmit stress worldwide - the August 2024 mini-crash was a preview.

stories.name: Private credit's opaque expansion

indicators.label: US high-yield OAS (%, ≈310bps)
Direct-lending default rate (%, Fitch incl. distressed exchanges)
Large-fund redemption gates (0 none / 1 isolated / 2 widespread)

stories.summary: Lending has migrated from banks to lightly regulated private-credit funds, where assets are marked infrequently and leverage is opaque. Defaults are rising from a low base; the risk is that losses surface suddenly rather than being visible in real time.

stories.name: Developing-world debt crisis

indicators.label: Broad US dollar index (FRED DTWEXBGS)
US 10y real yield (TIPS, %)
New IMF programs / missed coupons (0 calm / 1 rising / 2 cluster)

stories.summary: A strong dollar, high real rates, and heavy foreign-currency debt loads leave many developing economies vulnerable to a sudden stop. A cluster of sovereign defaults or new IMF programs would signal the slow-burn crisis turning acute.

stories.name: China's price spillover (deflation or cost-push)

indicators.label: China PPI YoY (%) - large swing either way is worse
USD/CNY (yuan depreciation = higher = risk)
New tariff/anti-dumping actions (0 calm / 1 rising / 2 escalating)

stories.summary: China's factory-gate prices spill into global goods markets in BOTH directions: years of PPI deflation exported disinflation and squeezed competitors, while a sharp 2026 reversal to positive PPI (energy/commodity cost-push) now exports input-cost pressure. Either large swing is destabilising; the indicator is scored on the size of the move, not its sign.

stories.name: Critical minerals as a weapon

indicators.label: Rare-earth export license flow (0 flowing / 1 slowing / 2 frozen)
Nov-2025 pause status (0 extended / 1 expiring / 2 lapsed)
US domestic RE producer blacklist (0 none / 1 entity-specific ban / 2 sector-wide ban)
Ex-China heavy rare-earth price premium (x China)

stories.summary: China dominates the mining and especially the processing of rare earths and critical minerals, and has shown willingness to use export licensing as leverage. Supply chains for magnets and defense inputs have little near-term substitute.

stories.name: Stablecoins & Treasury demand

indicators.label: Largest stablecoin max peg deviation (%)
Total USD stablecoin supply ($bn)
GENIUS implementation friction (0 smooth / 1 gaps / 2 problems)

stories.summary: Dollar stablecoins have become sizeable holders of short-term Treasuries, linking crypto plumbing to the funding market. A large redemption wave could force rapid T-bill selling; the GENIUS Act's implementation is the key regulatory variable.

stories.name: AI build-out circular financing

indicators.label: US investment-grade OAS (%) - big-issuer proxy
AI capex-vs-revenue gap concern (0 closing / 1 wide / 2 widening fast)
GPU-backed debt refinancing stress (0 none / 1 signs / 2 acute)

stories.summary: AI infrastructure spending vastly exceeds current AI revenue, increasingly financed with debt and circular vendor arrangements. If monetization disappoints or GPU-backed financing strains, the capex cycle could reverse sharply.

stories.name: CRE maturity wall / regional banks

indicators.label: CMBS office delinquency rate (%)
Regional-bank CRE stress (0 calm / 1 isolated / 2 cluster)

stories.summary: A wall of commercial real-estate loans - especially office - matures into higher rates and lower valuations, concentrated at regional banks. Rising delinquencies and 'extend and pretend' practices defer, rather than resolve, the losses.

stories.name: France / eurozone fragility

indicators.label: OAT-Bund 10y spread (%)
Govt stability (0 stable / 1 fragile / 2 collapse-or-snap-election)
Rating action (0 stable / 1 negative outlook / 2 downgrade)

stories.summary: France combines a wide deficit, a fragmented parliament, and recurring budget standoffs, widening its spread over Germany. Political instability or a rating downgrade would test eurozone cohesion at its second-largest economy.

stories.name: Hidden consumer debt

indicators.label: Subprime auto 60+ day delinquency (%)
US unemployment rate (%)
BNPL delinquency trend (0 stable / 1 rising / 2 spiking)

stories.summary: Beneath headline figures, subprime auto and buy-now-pay-later delinquencies are climbing, and the labor market is the swing factor. A rise in unemployment would convert stretched-but-current borrowers into defaults quickly.

stories.name: Gold / de-dollarization

indicators.label: Gold price (USD/oz)
USD share of FX reserves (%, IMF COFER)
Reserve-weaponization / settlement shift (0 none / 1 talk / 2 action)

stories.summary: Central banks are accumulating gold and building non-dollar settlement arrangements at the margin. It is a slow erosion rather than a sudden shift, but reserve 'weaponization' events can accelerate diversification away from the dollar.

stories.name: Insurance retreat

indicators.label: Insurer non-renewals / exits (0 stable / 1 rising / 2 accelerating)
US single-family mortgage delinquency (%, FRED DRSFRMACBS)
Catastrophe-loss pressure (0 normal / 1 elevated / 2 severe season)

stories.summary: Insurers are retreating from climate-exposed markets through non-renewals and exits, shifting risk onto homeowners and state backstops. Severe catastrophe seasons strain the system and feed into housing and mortgage stress.

stories.name: Pensions / demographics

indicators.label: Social Security / pension reform shock (0 none / 1 debate / 2 cuts)
Pension-fund leverage event, UK-2022 type (0 none / 1 stress / 2 blowup)
Large public-pension funded ratio (%)

stories.summary: Aging demographics and underfunded public pensions create slow fiscal pressure, while leveraged liability-driven strategies can blow up fast - as the UK gilt/LDI crisis showed in 2022. Benefit-reform fights are the political pressure valve.

stories.name: AI power & the grid bottleneck

indicators.label: Grid interconnection wait (months)
Data-center moratoria / backlash (0 none / 1 spreading / 2 widespread)
AI power-demand pressure (0 easing / 1 tight / 2 acute)

stories.summary: Data-center electricity demand is colliding with multi-year grid interconnection queues and slow capacity additions. Whether this is an acute shortfall or eases depends on the pace of AI build-out versus new supply - forecasts diverge widely.

stories.name: Copper & the electrification deficit

indicators.label: Copper price (USD/lb, COMEX HG=F)
Major mine disruptions (0 none / 1 some / 2 cluster)
Deficit timing (0 surplus / 1 balanced / 2 deficit)

stories.summary: Electrification and AI infrastructure point to structural copper deficits as demand outruns new mine supply, which takes a decade to build. Price is the live signal; mine disruptions and inventory draws would confirm tightening.

stories.name: Water - the underpriced input

indicators.label: Drought in a chip/farm hub (0 none / 1 emerging / 2 acute)
Key reservoir / basin stress (0 normal / 1 low / 2 critical)
Transboundary water dispute escalation (0 calm / 1 tense / 2 crisis)

stories.summary: Water is systematically underpriced yet essential to chip fabrication, agriculture, and power. Droughts in key hubs (Taiwan's fabs, major farming regions) and transboundary disputes can disrupt supply chains in ways markets rarely price in advance.

stories.name: Food & fertilizer fragility

indicators.label: Food-price trend (0 falling / 1 elevated / 2 spiking)
China fertilizer export curbs (0 lifted / 1 in place / 2 tightened)
Hormuz/Gulf disruption to fertilizer inputs (0 clear / 1 disrupted / 2 cut)

stories.summary: Food security depends on concentrated fertilizer supply chains - potash, phosphate, and gas-derived nitrogen - exposed to export curbs and shipping chokepoints. Curbs or input shocks feed through to prices with a lag.

stories.name: The lithography (ASML) chokepoint

indicators.label: Taiwan / cross-strait tension (0 calm / 1 elevated / 2 crisis)
Export-control escalation (0 stable / 1 tightening / 2 retaliation)
Single-point concentration (0 easing / 1 high / 2 extreme)

stories.summary: ASML is the sole maker of EUV lithography machines, with Zeiss the sole optics supplier - a single point of failure for advanced chips. Export controls, retaliation, or any disruption to this chain would ripple across the entire tech economy.

stories.name: Sea lanes & undersea cables

indicators.label: Hormuz/Red Sea status (0 open / 1 contested / 2 closed)
WTI crude oil (USD/bbl, CL=F)
Undersea cable incidents (0 none / 1 threatened / 2 cut)

stories.summary: A few maritime chokepoints and undersea cables carry most global trade and data. The 2026 Hormuz/Red Sea disruptions showed how quickly closures spike energy and shipping costs; cable cuts are a parallel, under-watched vulnerability.

stories.name: Clearinghouses (financial chokepoint)

indicators.label: Equity volatility (VIX)
Treasury volatility (MOVE)
Treasury-clearing rollout stress (0 smooth / 1 friction / 2 problems)

stories.summary: Central counterparties now concentrate the system's risk by design, and Treasury central-clearing mandates will route more activity through them. In a volatility spike, procyclical margin calls can amplify stress - they are a systemic single point of failure.

items.label: Direct-lending default rate (%, Fitch incl. distressed exchanges)
items.rationale: The 6.3% figure is the latest Fitch inclusive-measure print (counting distressed exchanges and maturity extensions as defaults), anchored to the same Fitch Private Credit Default Rate series that hit 6.0% in April 2026; no anchor switch is required as Fitch published a fresh August 2026 reading. The sequential rise from 6.0% (Apr/May) → 6.1% (Jul) → 6.3% (Aug) confirms the stress signal is intensifying, corroborated by rising PIK income at BDCs and elevated liability-management-exercise activity dominating default events.
items.fact: Fitch Ratings reported on Sept 14, 2026 that the trailing 12-month US private credit default rate (across ~1,300-1,500 borrowers, inclusive of distressed exchanges and maturity extensions) rose to 6.3% at end of August 2026, surpassing the prior record of 6.1% set in July 2026 and the April 2026 record of 6.0%; Fitch also recorded the highest monthly total of private credit default events in the trailing 12-month window. Sources: Bloomberg (Sept 14, 2026), Bitget/Fitch report summary (Sept 14, 2026), Epoch Times (Sept 15, 2026).

dissent.view: Proskauer Private Credit Default Index: 2.51% for Q2 2026 (count-based, senior secured/unitranche loans, ~716 loans / $195.6bn) — materially lower due to narrower borrower universe and exclusion of certain distressed exchanges

Moody's 2025 estimate: 1.6%-4.7% headline rate excluding distressed restructurings; estimates distressed restructurings accounted for ~65% of all 2025 private credit defaults — lower anchor methodology

items.label: GENIUS implementation friction (0 smooth / 1 gaps / 2 problems)
items.rationale: The rubric's level-2 condition is met without ambiguity: the statutory July 18, 2026 deadline passed with zero final rules in place across all required agencies, matching 'deadline missed without final rules.' No court stay or compliance-failure event is needed; the missed deadline alone satisfies the criterion.
items.fact: The GENIUS Act statutory deadline for final implementing rules was July 18, 2026. As of that date—and confirmed through at least September 2026—zero final rules had been issued by any of the six mandated agencies (OCC, FDIC, Federal Reserve, NCUA, Treasury/FinCEN/OFAC). All ten rule packages published during the first year remained in proposed/comment form. The OCC targets finalization by November 2026. Source: OCC Bulletin 2026-3 (occ.gov, Feb 25 2026); Federal Register FDIC NPRM (Apr 10 2026); Federal Register Treasury NPRM (Aug 18 2026, comments due Oct 19 2026); Crowdfund Insider (Jul 19 2026); crypto.news (Aug 2026).

dissent.view: Some analysts characterise the miss as operationally inconsequential because the GENIUS Act still takes effect January 18, 2027 regardless, and agencies continue rulemaking—implying a 'gaps' rather than 'problems' framing.

items.label: Large-fund redemption gates (0 none / 1 isolated / 2 widespread)
items.rationale: 10 of 16 Fitch-tracked BDCs gated in the same quarter (Q2 2026) is far above the rubric threshold of >=3 largest funds; combined AUM of BCRED + CCLFX + Apollo alone exceeds $135B, well above the $100B threshold for level 2. No corroborating signal is required for a structural cap-breach (these are contractual mechanisms, not discretionary gates), though equity prices of Blue Owl (-67%), Blackstone (-46%), Apollo (-41%) and KKR/Ares (-48%) confirm market-wide stress corroborating the redemption pressure.
items.fact: Fitch Ratings data (cited Aug 2026 by Angel Investors Network/CoinDesk): 10 of 16 tracked non-traded BDCs breached their 5% quarterly redemption caps in Q2 2026; named funds include Blackstone BCRED (~$79-82B AUM), Apollo Debt Solutions BDC (~$25B), Ares Strategic Income Fund (~$10.7B), Blue Owl OTIC, Blue Owl OBDC II (fully halted Feb 2026), Oaktree Strategic Credit, Cliffwater CCLFX (~$31B), HPS HLEND, BlackRock BDEBT, and Variant Investments. Robert A. Stanger & Co. (Aug 17 2026) puts Q2 repurchase requests at 12.4% of NAV - highest ever recorded - with only 38% fulfilled and ~$9.6B in requests unfilled.

items.label: Takaichi plan financing clarity (0 ok / 1 unclear / 2 disorderly)
items.rationale: The 10y yield has surged well above 25bps from its early-2026 level on explicit fiscal concern (rubric threshold for score 1), but auctions are still clearing with bid-to-cover above 3 and no emergency BOJ operation has been reported, ruling out score 2 (disorderly). The funding path for the ¥143 trillion FY2027 budget request remains unspecified, satisfying the secondary score-1 condition.
items.fact: Japan 10-year JGB yield reached 3.000% on 1 September 2026 (30-year high, up ~90bps from ~2.1% in March 2026) driven by Takaichi fiscal expansion fears and a record ¥143 trillion FY2027 budget request. As of 18 September 2026 the yield eased to 2.99% (TradingEconomics). The 30-year auction on 3 September 2026 cleared with a bid-to-cover of 3.79 vs. 12-month average of 3.52 (Bloomberg, 3 Sep 2026). No failed auction or emergency BOJ operation reported; HSBC noted 'limited clarity on funding channels' with 'additional debt issuance a plausible outcome' (CNBC, 4 Aug 2026).

dissent.view: Universal Asset Owners Probability Desk (1 Sep 2026) argues the 3% yield breach is a 'term-premium event, not a fiscal crisis,' citing robust 10y auction demand on the same day yields hit 3%

Oxford Economics raised end-2026 10y JGB forecast to 2.8%, viewing risks as 'more balanced' after June supplementary budget came in smaller than feared—implying less stress than headline yields suggest

items.label: Treasury-clearing rollout stress (0 smooth / 1 friction / 2 problems)
items.rationale: Pending exemptive relief on inter-affiliate and extraterritorial scope, a documented legal/documentation backlog per TBAC, and a readiness confidence level of 54% (cash) — below the rubric's 60% threshold — all map squarely to rubric level 1 (FRICTION). No deadline extension or operational failure has been confirmed, precluding level 2.
items.fact: TBAC's May 2026 charge paper states 'the largest challenge from an implementation standpoint continues to be the amount of legal work and documentation associated with bilateral agreements between participants,' and the SEC's August 7 2026 statement still urges firms to 'continue their efforts to prepare for a smooth and successful transition by the current deadline.' SIFMA's exemptive relief request for inter-affiliate and extraterritorial scope remained pending in comment as of August 2026, with the SEC's Rule 15c3-3 net omnibus margin notice also open. The Nov 2025 SIFMA/DTCC/Broadridge pulse survey (330 firms) found only 54% of firms 'very confident' of cash-deadline readiness and 40% for repo. (Sources: TBAC Charge Q2 2026 PDF, SEC.gov August 2026 statement, SIFMA/Broadridge Pulse Survey Nov 2025)

dissent.view: SEC Chair Atkins confirmed in March 2026 the December 2026 cash deadline remains intact and is 'important to achieve for market integrity,' suggesting no imminent extension — potentially a more sanguine read than level 1.
TBAC May 2026 notes 'the cash market is relatively better positioned vs repo' due to narrower scope and more developed done-away structure, implying cash friction is moderate rather than severe.

items.label: AI capex-vs-revenue gap concern (0 closing / 1 wide / 2 widening fast)
items.rationale: Capex growth (~77-84% YoY) clearly outpaces AI-attributable cloud revenue growth (~48% YoY), ruling out Score 0. However, AI-revenue growth accelerated QoQ (39% in Q1 to 48% in Q2) and all hyperscalers describe themselves as supply-constrained rather than demand-constrained, ruling out Score 2; this is the canonical Score 1 configuration.
items.fact: Q2 CY2026 earnings (SEC 8-K Alphabet July 22 2026; Amazon/FourWeekMBA July 31 2026): Google Cloud +82% YoY to $24.8B, AWS +37% to $42.2B, Azure +43% constant-currency — aggregate hyperscaler cloud/AI revenue growth ~48% YoY, accelerating from ~39% in Q1. Simultaneously, combined 2026 capex guidance was raised again post-Q2 to ~$775–800B (up ~77–84% YoY from ~$413B in 2025); Amazon Q2 quarterly capex alone was $54.2B, Alphabet $44.9B. Capex growth (~77-84%) materially exceeds AI-revenue growth (~48%).

dissent.view: Sequoia (David Cahn, 2025 estimate still cited as of mid-2026) estimated a ~$600B annual gap between AI infrastructure spend and AI ecosystem revenue — broader than just hyperscaler cloud, suggesting the macro monetisation gap is larger than cloud revenue growth alone implies

Moody's May 2026 forecast revision flagged credit risk if 'strong profit growth from AI investments fails to materialise,' a more cautious read implying potential Score 2 trajectory if depreciation lands 2027-28

items.label: BNPL delinquency trend (0 stable / 1 rising / 2 spiking)
items.rationale: 30+ DPD is modestly up YoY (+18 bps per Q2 FY2026 filing) and the FY2026 curve sits slightly above FY2025, satisfying 'late-payment/delinquency up YoY'; however charge-offs remain ~1.8%-2%, well below the 3% ceiling for rating=1 and far below the 5% spike threshold for rating=2. The +18 bps YoY rise is also well short of the >100 bps needed for rating=2.
items.fact: Affirm 30+ DPD on monthly installment loans (ex-Peloton, ex-Pay-in-X) was 2.5% in Q4 FY2026 (ended June 30, 2026), improving from 2.7%-2.8% over the prior three quarters; Q2 FY2026 filing reported 30+ DPD up +18 bps YoY at 2.7%. FY2026 delinquency curve tracked slightly above FY2025. Industry BNPL charge-off rate ~1.83% per CFPB Dec-2025 report (latest official figure). Source: Affirm Q4 FY2026 IR release (investors.affirm.com, Aug 27 2026); Affirm Q2 FY2026 shareholder letter (Feb 2026); Richmond Fed EB-26-05 (Feb 2026).

dissent.view: BTIG Research (Aug 21, 2026) flagged Affirm ABS 2025-X2 vintage 30-59 DPD at all-time highs at 9 and 16 months of age, suggesting deterioration in newer cohorts that may not yet be fully reflected in reported portfolio-level delinquency

items.label: CMBS office delinquency rate (%)
items.rationale: The rubric calls for the latest Trepp CMBS office delinquency rate as a percent; 11.76% is the last openly published Trepp office figure, from October 2025. KBRA data for Jan-Feb 2026 shows office delinquency rising further to 12.8–13.9%, suggesting the Trepp figure has likely also climbed, but absent a confirmed 2026 Trepp office print, 11.76% is the anchor with medium confidence. [vintage guard: new read is 2025-10-31 data but the prior applied value was 2026-03 data; kept the newer vintage]
items.fact: Trepp CMBS office delinquency rate hit an all-time high of 11.76% in October 2025, per CommercialSearch/Trepp tracker (commercialsearch.com, 'the office sector soared 63 basis points in October to set a new all-time high of 11.76 percent'). The most recent publicly available Trepp overall CMBS rate for August 2026 is 7.85% (Multifamily Dive, Sept. 16 2026), with office still the dominant delinquent sector (~42% of late-paying balance per Connect CRE, Sept. 10 2026), but no updated Trepp office-specific percentage for 2026 was found in open sources.

items.label: GPU-backed debt refinancing stress (0 none / 1 signs / 2 acute)
items.rationale: Banks are actively offloading AI/data-center-backed debt at a discount and CoreWeave - a named GPU-backed borrower with $35B debt as of Q2 2026 - is facing a documented refinancing wall with CDS pricing at deeply distressed levels; these are textbook Level 1 SIGNS. However, no deal has actually failed or defaulted, so Level 2 is not warranted.
items.fact: As of July-August 2026: (1) JPMorgan, Morgan Stanley, and SMBC spent 6+ months attempting to distribute ~$38B in Oracle-linked data-center construction debt, with some banks selling portions at a discount (TechNewsday/ResultSense, May 6 2026); (2) CoreWeave (Nasdaq: CRWV) CDS hit ~855 bps on July 29 2026, implying ~50% five-year default probability, while its $2.6B leveraged loan required improved terms to clear (metirai.com/TechTimes, July 29-Aug 2 2026). No confirmed default, distressed exchange, or failed refinancing has been reported.

dissent.view: CoreWeave completed its $8.5B DDTL-4.0 facility (March 2026) and a $3.1B deal in Q3, suggesting lenders are still extending GPU-backed credit at scale despite CDS distress signals - some analysts read this as functioning, not stressed, refinancing.

items.label: Insurer non-renewals / exits (0 stable / 1 rising / 2 accelerating)
items.rationale: The NAIC data and corroborating sources confirm elevated non-renewal waves spanning well more than 5 states (credibly 10-15+ named states) across all four US regions, but the NAIC simultaneously characterizes the market as 'operationally strong overall with broad insurer participation and improved underwriting results in 2024,' and no single top-10 insurer has executed a full state-market exit in 2026 — placing the indicator squarely in the RISING band (5-15 states, some markets stabilizing).
items.fact: NAIC's Aug 5, 2026 first-of-its-kind national report ('Examining Homeowner Property Insurance Market Dynamics: An Assessment of Countrywide State-Level Data From 2018 to 2024') found insurer-initiated nonrenewal rates surged 96%-216% across all four US regions (Southeast, Northeast, Midwest, West) since 2018; Florida non-renewed 3.35% of policies in 2024 (highest in nation), California 3.18%; non-renewal/market-exit stress documented across CA, FL, LA, CO, TX, GA, OK, MN and others — a third-party tally (Climate Cosmos, June 2026) cited 13 named states with active non-renewal waves. NAIC, content.naic.org, Aug 5, 2026.

dissent.view: NAIC Aug 2026 report says market 'remains operationally strong overall, with broad insurer participation and improved underwriting results in 2024,' suggesting stress is elevated but not systemic/accelerating.

Climate Cosmos (June 2026) counted 13 named states with active insurer non-renewal waves, which approaches the upper end of the RISING band and could support a score of 2 if additional state-level exits materialize in H2 2026.

items.label: Regional-bank CRE stress (0 calm / 1 isolated / 2 cluster)
items.rationale: Within the trailing 6 months (Mar 22-Sep 22 2026), 1-2 failures occurred with at most one (Metropolitan Capital, at the edge of the window) having a credible CRE-link per Bisnow reporting, while FDIC 2026 Risk Review constitutes a public supervisory statement citing regional-bank CRE concentration; no failure exceeded $10B and no coordinated interagency action was issued, placing this squarely in ISOLATED (score=1). [cross-check (asi1): two reads disagreed (1 vs 0); held for review]
items.fact: Five US banks failed in 2026 YTD (Metropolitan Capital Bank & Trust $261M Jan 30; Community Bank and Trust-West Georgia May 1; Kentland Federal Savings Jul 10; Small Business Bank of Lenexa ~Jul 17; Tioga-Franklin Savings Bank $68M Aug 21); all were sub-$100M except Metropolitan Capital. Bisnow (Feb 2, 2026) identified a CRE/skilled-nursing-facility loan as a contributing factor at Metropolitan Capital via court records, though FDIC did not publicly cite CRE as cause. FDIC Quarterly Banking Profile (Aug 25, 2026) characterizes the industry as broadly sound; D&O Diary (Sep 2026) citing Law.com concludes 2026 failures are idiosyncratic. FDIC 2026 Risk Review (Apr 2026) flags ongoing CRE credit risk monitoring for regional banks. No coordinated interagency CRE emergency facility issued. Sources: fdic.gov/bank-failures/failed-bank-list (Aug 21, 2026 last update); americanbanker.com (Aug 21, 2026); dandodiary.com (Sep 2026); bisnow.com (Feb 2, 2026); fdic.gov/analysis/2026-risk-review (Apr 2026).

items.label: Subprime auto 60+ day delinquency (%)
items.rationale: The rubric calls for the latest reported subprime auto 60+ day delinquency rate as a percent; the July 2026 Fitch ABS index reading of 6.13% is the most recent hard figure from an authoritative ABS-tracker source, mechanically mapping to 6.13. The seasonal pattern (H2 deterioration after H1 tax-refund relief) corroborates the direction of the print.
items.fact: Fitch Auto ABS subprime 60-plus-day delinquency index: 5.80% in June 2026, then jumped 33 basis points to 6.13% in July 2026, per CUCollector citing Fitch Auto ABS indices (published ~Sep 22, 2026).

dissent.view: KBRA July 2026 Auto Loan ABS report shows non-prime 60+ day delinquency rose 19 bps from June and 26 bps year-over-year — directionally consistent but covers a slightly broader 'non-prime' universe, implying a somewhat different absolute level
ankso.blog (Sep 2026) cites Fitch subprime 60+ delinquency at 5.49% for May 2026 — consistent with the seasonal trough but one month earlier than the July reversal

items.label: Large public-pension funded ratio (%)
items.rationale: The Milliman PPFI is the most frequently updated, authoritative aggregate measure for the 100 largest U.S. public pension plans; the July 31, 2026 reading of 88.2% is the latest published data point and maps directly to the rubric's request for a representative large-plan funded ratio. A dissenting lower median (~73-75%) from NASRA/actuarial valuations reflects older measurement-date liability snapshots and plan-reported actuarial assumptions rather than current market values.
items.fact: Milliman 100 Public Pension Funding Index (PPFI): funded ratio of the 100 largest U.S. public pension plans = 88.2% as of July 31, 2026. Published by Milliman on August 27, 2026. Source: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260827829119/en/Milliman-analysis-Public-pension-funded-ratio-slips-again-to-88.2-as-of-July-31

dissent.view: NASRA median funded ratio for U.S. public pensions approximately 73-75% as of 2024-2025, using plan-reported actuarial valuations rather than current market values
Equable Institute 'State of Pensions 2026' reports overall status as 'Fragile' with ~31% of plans in Resilient status and ~10% Distressed; NJ at 56.7% and IL at 56.4% among worst

items.label: New IMF programs / missed coupons (0 calm / 1 rising / 2 cluster)
items.rationale: Zero confirmed new IMF distress-driven programs or missed coupons among EM sovereigns in the trailing 6 months maps mechanically to CALM (0) under the rubric. The IMF's own public characterisation of EM resilience at its Spring 2026 meetings reinforces the absence of a cluster or single-event trigger.
items.fact: No new EM sovereign missed coupon, standstill, or new IMF distress-driven program was identified in authoritative sources for the March–September 2026 window. IMF MD Georgieva at Spring Meetings 2026 (April 15, 2026, imf.org) characterised EM balance sheets as broadly resilient with 'independent central banks, fiscal councils, built very strong reserves.' The IMF/World Bank joint statement of September 21, 2026 (Reuters/WHBL) cited structural LIC debt-distress metrics but announced no new EM sovereign program or missed coupon. Congo's March 2026 IMF assessment was a post-financing review of a legacy program, not a new distress arrangement.

dissent.view: IMF/World Bank (Sept 21 2026) note ~14% of LICs are 'in debt distress' and ~23% of EM countries 'at high risk of overall sovereign stress' -- elevated risk rhetoric, but no specific new program or missed coupon is named; risk ≠ executed distress event under the rubric.

items.label: Rating action (0 stable / 1 negative outlook / 2 downgrade)
items.rationale: Two Big Three agencies (Fitch, S&P) executed actual one-notch rating cuts within the trailing 12 months (Sep-Oct 2025), satisfying rubric level 2 unambiguously. Moody's additionally holds a negative outlook as of Apr 2026, reinforcing the most-severe classification.
items.fact: Fitch downgraded France from AA- to A+ (stable outlook) on 12 Sep 2025; S&P downgraded France from AA- to A+ (stable outlook) on 18 Oct 2025; Moody's downgraded France from Aa2 to Aa3 in Dec 2024 and on 11 Apr 2026 maintained Aa3 with a NEGATIVE outlook. All three actions are within or overlap the trailing 12 months to 22 Sep 2026. Sources: Bloomberg (10 Sep 2025), France24 (18 Oct 2025), Xinhua/Moody's (11 Apr 2026).

dissent.view: S&P confirmed A+ with stable outlook in May 2026 and Fitch upheld A+ stable in Mar 2026, so on a forward-looking basis both are stable—could argue level 1 (Moody's negative outlook) if one counts only current outlooks rather than trailing cuts.

items.label: Reserve-weaponization / settlement shift (0 none / 1 talk / 2 action)
items.rationale: The New Delhi Declaration constitutes new multilateral official endorsement of non-dollar settlement architecture (BRICS Pay mandate, local-currency settlement), meeting the rubric definition of Level 1 TALK. No new sovereign reserve freeze or seizure of a new target occurred in 2026, and BRICS Pay remains in pilot/expansion phase rather than operationally displacing USD settlement for a major economy, precluding Level 2.
items.fact: The 18th BRICS Summit New Delhi Declaration (12-13 Sep 2026) formally endorsed expansion of the BRICS Payment Task Force mandate for local-currency cross-border settlements and BRICS Pay, but adopted no common currency and launched no operationally live reserve-settlement system displacing USD; no new sovereign reserve freeze or seizure beyond the pre-existing 2022 Russian asset freeze was executed (sources: Wikipedia 18th BRICS Summit; entrepreneurloop.com BRICS 2026 takeaways; deepmentor.co New Delhi Declaration summary, Sep 2026).

dissent.view: Some secondary sources (informedclearly.com, watcher.guru) characterise BRICS Pay as having 'gone live' or 'operationally launched' in 2026, which could imply Level 2; however, authoritative summit outcome documents and EBC/Irish Times reporting confirm the system remains in pilot/expansion phase with no common currency and no major economy formally moving reserve settlement off USD.

items.label: Social Security / pension reform shock (0 none / 1 debate / 2 cuts)
items.rationale: The trustees report worsened the OASI depletion date (moved earlier to Q4 2032) and the 75-year shortfall grew materially, satisfying rubric band 1 ('trustees report worsens the depletion date or reform actively debated'). No automatic cut has been triggered and no enacted legislation reduces benefits, so band 2 is not met.
items.fact: The 2026 Social Security Trustees Report (released June 9, 2026; primary source: ssa.gov/oact/TR/2026/tr2026.pdf) projects the OASI trust fund will be depleted in Q4 2032 -- one quarter earlier than the prior year's estimate -- at which point only 78% of scheduled benefits would be payable (a ~22% automatic cut). The combined OASDI depletion date remains 2034 (83% payable). The 75-year actuarial deficit widened to 4.42% of taxable payroll. Multiple reform bills (Bipartisan Social Security Commission Act H.R. 9187; PROMISE Act, introduced July 14, 2026) are in debate but none has been enacted. No automatic benefit reduction has been triggered and no legislation cutting benefits has been signed into law.

dissent.view: CBO (February 2026) independently estimated the 2032 depletion date but projects a steeper 28% automatic cut vs. the trustees' 22%, reflecting different economic assumptions.

items.label: USD share of FX reserves (%, IMF COFER)

items.fact: IMF COFER Data Brief (data.imf.org, published ~July 1 2026): 'The share of US dollar holdings in foreign exchange reserves increased to 57.13 percent in 2026Q1, from 56.42 percent in 2025Q4.' USD claims = $7,486.93bn of total ~$13.1tn allocated reserves.

items.label: Export-control escalation (0 stable / 1 tightening / 2 retaliation)
items.rationale: Both sides have enacted new measures in the trailing 3 months: the US tightened via BIS guidance (June 2026) and the MATCH Act legislative push, while China enacted two formal counter-control regulations (Order 834 and Extraterritorial Jurisdiction rules) plus rare-earth escalation, satisfying rubric level 2 (RETALIATION). US-side measures: BIS June 2026 subsidiary guidance, MATCH Act advancing. China-side measures: Order 834 (Apr 2026), Extraterritorial Jurisdiction Regulation (Apr 2026), rare-earth export control escalation (Jun-Jul 2026).
items.fact: Within the trailing 3 months: (1) US-side: BIS issued June 1 2026 guidance affirming chip export restrictions extend to Chinese firms' overseas subsidiaries (Al Jazeera, 1 Jun 2026); MATCH Act (introduced Apr 2 2026) advancing in Congress with Senate version in parallel, targeting DUV immersion lithography and servicing bans. items.label: Nov-2025 pause status (0 extended / 1 expiring / 2 lapsed)
items.rationale: Two independent rubric-1 triggers are satisfied: the truce is inside the <90-day-to-expiry window with no confirmed renewal, and China's June 2026 entity-list additions against US rare-earth miners constitute a partial breach. The truce has not formally lapsed (ruling out Score 2), but fraying is well-documented.
items.fact: China's Oct-2025 rare earth export controls remain suspended until Nov 10, 2026 (White House fact sheet, Nov 5 2025; China-Briefing, Nov 7 2025), but as of Sept 22, 2026 no renewal has been announced (<49 days to expiry), USTR Greer said parties 'remain divided' on extension terms (Bloomberg, Sept 21 2026), and China added 10 US rare-earth firms (incl. MP Materials, USA Rare Earth) to new entity restrictions in June 2026 (Reuters, cited by Modern Diplomacy, Aug 21 2026).

items.label: Rare-earth export license flow (0 flowing / 1 slowing / 2 frozen)
items.rationale: The rubric scores 1 (SLOWING) when licensing is case-by-case or whitelist-only AND/OR typical processing exceeds 30 days AND/OR a new category was added in the trailing 3 months. All three conditions are met: licensing is case-by-case except for three whitelisted exporters; real approval times are 60-120 days; and new catalogue additions (samarium/gadolinium/lutetium compounds) took effect January 2026. A score of 2 is not warranted because licences continue to be issued for civilian/commercial end-users and no categorical country-level denial or formal suspension of licensing has been announced.
items.fact: As of September 2026, China's MOFCOM operates a mandatory case-by-case export licensing regime for seven heavy/medium REE categories and associated magnets (April 2025 Wave 1, fully enforced). General licences were issued in December 2025 to only three named major Chinese magnet makers (JL MAG, San Huan, Yunsheng) and are not broadly available. Real processing times run 60-120 days for heavy-REE approvals, well above the 45-working-day statutory target. August 2026 magnet shipments fell 21% month-on-month to ~512 metric tons, corroborating selective/slow approvals. The 2026 licensing catalogue added samarium, gadolinium, and lutetium compounds as new controlled categories (effective January 2026). Sources: discoveryalert.com (Sept 22 2026 customs data); duramag.com (2025-2026 market update); certivo.com (March 2026); mining.com (Dec 2025 Reuters-cited general licence report); china-briefing.com (updated Nov 2025).

dissent.view: MOFCOM and Global Times (June 2025) characterise the system as open and compliant, stating China 'will approve applications that meet requirements'; Trump administration claimed a June 2026 bilateral deal substantially eased approvals, though MOFCOM's confirmation was partial and China Briefing notes no substantive procedural change is confirmed.

China-briefing (updated Nov 2025) notes that MOFCOM stated it would 'review and approve eligible export applications' under the US-China trade truce, implying a more permissive posture than the market-restriction narrative; but acknowledges it 'remains unclear' whether this changed actual processing.

items.label: Single-point concentration (0 easing / 1 high / 2 extreme)

The Arizona 4nm fab (Phase 1) does not qualify as <=3nm, and both overseas 3nm fabs remain pre-production.

The operational Kumamoto Fab 1 runs 12-28nm only. Source: TSMC Q1 2026 earnings call (CC Wei, April 16 2026) via TrendForce/mlq.ai; tsmc.com Arizona page (July 2026); TechTimes Aug 8 2026; TrendForce Sept 14 2026.

items.label: Taiwan / cross-strait tension (0 calm / 1 elevated / 2 crisis)
items.rationale: Persistent PLAN/coast-guard vessel presence at record levels plus recent live-fire drills and continued daily median-line crossings constitute large-scale assertive activity well above routine, matching rubric level 1; no kinetic clash, no enforced blockade, and no full mobilization has been documented, precluding level 2.

Source: Utility Dive (May 19, 2026, https://www.utilitydive.com/news/pjm-doe-emergency-order-curtail-data-centers/820571/) and TechTimes (July 4, 2026, https://www.techtimes.com/articles/319678/20260704/ai-data-centers-trigger-third-federal-grid-emergency-sending-bills-up-air-quality-down.htm).

items.fact: SEC Final Rule 34-102487 (Feb 25, 2025) granted a one-year extension of compliance dates to Dec 31, 2026 (cash) and Jun 30, 2027 (repo); additionally, on Apr 17, 2026, the SEC published SIFMA's exemptive-relief request for an expanded inter-affiliate exemption (SEC Release 34-105262). No second extension has been announced as of Sep 2026. Source: sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2025-43; sec.gov/newsroom/speeches-statements/uyeda-update-sec-work-toward-treasury-clearing-implementation-042026; Treasury TBAC Charge Q2 2026 (May 2026).

items.label: Catastrophe-loss pressure (0 normal / 1 elevated / 2 severe season)
items.rationale: YTD global insured losses of ~$42-47bn are below - not above - the 10-year H1 average of ~$50bn, and no single event has crossed the $10bn threshold; the hurricane season is historically quiet under El Nino suppression with zero hurricane formations through mid-September. Both rubric triggers for score 1 (YTD above average OR single event >$10bn) are absent, placing the indicator firmly at 0 (NORMAL).
items.fact: Global insured catastrophe losses reached ~$42-47bn in H1 2026 (Swiss Re: $42bn, 16% below 10-year average; Munich Re: $44bn, below 10-year H1 average of $50bn; Aon: $47bn), with no single event exceeding $10bn. The 2026 Atlantic hurricane season is 'extremely inactive' as of September 2026 with no hurricane formed through Sept 11 (the latest first-hurricane date in the satellite era), driven by a strong El Nino. Sources: Swiss Re Institute H1 2026 sigma (Aug 2026), Munich Re H1 2026 nat cat report (Jul 30 2026), Aon H1 2026 Global Cat Recap (Jul 22 2026), Wikipedia 2026 Atlantic hurricane season.

items.label: Govt stability (0 stable / 1 fragile / 2 collapse-or-snap-election)
items.rationale: France has a minority/hung parliament (no party holds an absolute majority since the 2024 snap election); the government explicitly relied on Article 49.3 and survived multiple no-confidence votes in Jan-Feb 2026, the textbook definition of Rubric 1 (FRAGILE). No dissolution or government collapse has occurred since Oct 2025.
items.fact: The Second Lecornu government (formed 10 Oct 2025) is the incumbent minority coalition government of France. On 23 Jan 2026, PM Lecornu invoked Article 49.3 to pass the revenue section of the 2026 budget without a vote; two subsequent no-confidence motions (LFI: 269 votes, RN: fewer) both failed to reach the 288-vote threshold, saved by Socialist and conservative abstentions. The budget was formally adopted ~2 Feb 2026. Government remains in office as a minority. Sources: Wikipedia/Second Lecornu government; Euronews 23 Jan 2026; Al Jazeera 2 Feb 2026; Stratfor/RANE 23 Jan 2026.

items.label: Pension-fund leverage event, UK-2022 type (0 none / 1 stress / 2 blowup)
items.rationale: TPR and ESMA confirm LDI buffers are adequate (≥250-300 bps, well above the ~140 bps trigger seen in 2022) and no regulator has flagged a new margin-call episode or forced gilt selling in 2025-2026; this maps to Rubric 0 (buffers adequate, no margin stress). Confidence is medium rather than high because the most recent TPR data runs only to March 2025 and no real-time Q3 2026 regulatory statement was found.
items.fact: TPR Market Oversight report (thepensionsregulator.gov.uk, data to March 2025) confirms LDI market shrank from ~£1.5tn to ~£0.7tn, rate buffers rebuilt to ~300 bps, and 'LDI arrangements remained resilient in January 2025 when gilt yields increased.' ESMA June 2026 paper reviews post-2022 regulatory framework with no new stress episode flagged.

items.label: China PPI YoY (%) - large swing either way is worse
items.rationale: The rubric requires the signed NBS figure: +3.8% for August 2026, released 2026-09-09. This is a meaningfully positive reading—well above zero—signalling cost-push input-price pressure that can export inflationary spillovers to China's trading partners; the engine scores on magnitude, not sign.
items.fact: China PPI year-on-year for August 2026 = +3.8%, as published by the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS) on 9 September 2026. CNBC: 'The producer price index increased 3.8%, according to data released by the National Bureau of Statistics on Wednesday, exceeding economists forecast for a 3.6% gain.' People's Daily / NBS confirmed the same figure; NBS statistician Dong Lijuan cited imported commodity price pressures and high-tech demand as drivers.

items.label: US domestic RE producer blacklist (0 none / 1 entity-specific ban / 2 sector-wide ban)
items.rationale: Two named US rare-earth producers (MP Materials, USA Rare Earth) are explicitly on China's MOFCOM export-control list as of 22 June 2026, satisfying Rubric 1 exactly; every primary source characterises the measure as entity-specific, not a sector-wide or categorical ban, ruling out Rubric 2.
items.fact: China MOFCOM Announcement No. 23 of 2026 (issued 22 June 2026) added 10 named US entities to its export-control list under the Export Control Law and Regulations on Dual-Use Items, including MP Materials Corp. and USA Rare Earth, Inc., prohibiting Chinese suppliers from exporting dual-use items to those specific firms. Multiple corroborating sources (Benchmark Minerals, Al Jazeera, Reuters/Bloomberg via StockTitan, SMM) confirm the listing is entity-specific and not a categorical ban on the US rare-earth sector. Share-price reaction on listing day was muted (MP roughly flat, USA Rare Earth modestly higher), consistent with an entity-specific rather than sector-wide action.

items.label: China fertilizer export curbs (0 lifted / 1 in place / 2 tightened)
items.rationale: Existing urea quotas and phosphate suspensions remain operative structures (rubric band 1); the March 2026 expansion to NK blends/phosphates was a tightening but falls outside the trailing 3-month window (pre-June 22), and within that window China actually loosened the urea component (expanded allowance, surging July shipments), precluding band 2.
items.fact: As of early September 2026, China expanded its 2026 urea export allowance to roughly 5-5.5 million tonnes (up from an initial 3.3Mt cap) and July shipments surged to ~403,000t from just 7,000t in June; phosphate export curbs (DAP, MAP, certain NPK) imposed since mid-March 2026 were extended at least through August 2026 per NDRC guidance reported by S&P Global/Platts (Dec 2025) and confirmed by FertilizerDaily (July 29, 2026). A quota-and-suspension regime on urea and phosphate thus remains active, with no confirmed full lift as of the assessment date. Sources: FertilizerDaily 2026-09-09 (urea $443/t, China shipments surge); FertilizerDaily 2026-07-29 (phosphate curbs through Aug 2026); S&P Global/Platts 2026-03-04 (NDRC phosphate suspension).

items.label: Food-price trend (0 falling / 1 elevated / 2 spiking)
items.rationale: MoM gain of 1.9% and positive YoY confirm ELEVATED (rising), but the 1.9% MoM is below the 3% upper bound for band 1 and far below the 5% SPIKING threshold; no 3-month window reaches +10% on the composite index.
items.fact: FAO FFPI averaged 133.3 points in August 2026, up 1.9% MoM from revised July level of ~130.8 and up 2.5% YoY; highest since late 2022. Source: FAO newsroom, fao.org, released 4 September 2026.

flags.name: Two Hormuz reads disagree on the same strait
flags.message: Gulf fertilizer inputs are rated CUT (2, i.e. closure) but the sea-lane indicator rates the very same Strait of Hormuz only CONTESTED (<=1). They track one physical chokepoint and must agree - align the fertilizer read down to DISRUPTED (1) unless the strait is genuinely closed.

flags.message: Large-fund redemption gates are rated WIDESPREAD (2) but high-yield spreads are benign. Broad gating usually coincides with visible credit stress; confirm the gates are systemic, not a couple of isolated funds.

s1_basis_trade.label: Hidden leverage in US government bonds
s1_basis_trade.gist: Hedge funds borrow heavily to trade US government bonds; if that trade unwinds fast it can freeze the market everyone treats as safe.

s2_japan.label: Japan's rates and the global cash carry trade
s2_japan.gist: Cheap Japanese money has funded bets worldwide for years; as Japan's interest rates rise, pulling that money home can ripple through global markets.

s3_private_credit.label: Private lending you can't see into
s3_private_credit.gist: A fast-growing pile of loans sits outside the banks with little public disclosure, so stress there is hard to spot until it is already large.

s4_dev_debt.label: Debt stress in developing countries
s4_dev_debt.gist: Many poorer nations owe more than they can comfortably repay; a wave of defaults can spread and pull in their lenders.

s5_china_deflation.label: China's prices spilling into the world
s5_china_deflation.gist: Big swings in China's factory prices - falling or rising - get exported to everyone else as cheaper goods or higher input costs.

s6_rare_earths.label: Rare-earth minerals used as a weapon
s6_rare_earths.gist: China controls most of the world's rare-earth processing and is now restricting it, squeezing US defense and high-tech manufacturing.

s7_stablecoins.label: Crypto dollars and US government debt
s7_stablecoins.gist: Stablecoins must hold US Treasuries as backing, so their rapid growth - or a sudden wobble - now feeds straight back into the government-debt market.

s8_ai_capex.label: The AI spending boom
s8_ai_capex.gist: Enormous borrowing to build AI data centers is racing ahead of the revenue meant to justify it, concentrating the risk in a few giant companies.

s9_cre.label: Commercial real estate and small banks
s9_cre.gist: Half-empty offices and loans coming due strain the regional banks that hold them - a slow-burning credit risk.

s10_france.label: France and eurozone stability
s10_france.gist: A politically gridlocked, heavily indebted France is the soft spot that could reopen broader euro-area stress.

s11_consumer_debt.label: Household debt strain
s11_consumer_debt.gist: Rising late payments on car loans and buy-now-pay-later show households stretching - an early warning on consumer health.

s12_gold_dedollar.label: Gold and moving away from the dollar
s12_gold_dedollar.gist: Central banks stockpiling gold and building non-dollar payment systems slowly chip away at the dollar's dominance.

s13_insurance.label: Insurers pulling back
s13_insurance.gist: As disaster losses climb, insurers raise prices or quit whole regions, leaving homes and assets exposed.

s14_pensions.label: Pensions and an aging population
s14_pensions.gist: Aging populations and underfunded pensions strain public budgets; leveraged pension funds can also break in a sudden rate shock, as the UK saw in 2022.

s15_ai_power.label: AI's strain on the power grid
s15_ai_power.gist: AI data centers need more electricity than the grid can quickly supply, triggering curtailments, building moratoria, and multi-year connection queues.

s16_copper.label: Copper for electrification
s16_copper.gist: Electrifying everything needs far more copper than mines can deliver, and major mine outages are tightening supply further.

s17_water.label: Water as a hidden constraint
s17_water.gist: Droughts and shrinking reservoirs threaten chip factories, farms, and power generation - an underpriced input with no substitute.

s18_food_fertilizer.label: Food and fertilizer supply
s18_food_fertilizer.gist: Export curbs and shipping disruptions to fertilizer raise the risk of higher food prices down the line.

s19_lithography.label: The chipmaking chokepoint
s19_lithography.gist: The most advanced chips depend on one Dutch tool-maker and Taiwan's factories; any disruption there hits the entire tech economy.

s20_sea_lanes.label: Shipping lanes and undersea cables
s20_sea_lanes.gist: Key straits like Hormuz and the undersea cables carrying the internet are vulnerable chokepoints for global trade and data.

s21_clearinghouses.label: The financial system's plumbing
s21_clearinghouses.gist: Clearinghouses sit at the center of every market; if one seized up under stress, it would jam trading everywhere at once.

playbook.disclaimer: Educational cause-and-effect only - how stress like this has historically moved through the system. Nothing here is investment advice or a prediction.

s1_basis_trade.mechanism: A rates shock forces highly leveraged government-bond arbitrage positions to unwind at once: margin calls trigger forced Treasury selling, liquidity in the world's benchmark market evaporates, and everything priced off it reprices.
benefits: cash and short-term bills through the panic
long-term government bonds AFTER central-bank intervention
s1_basis_trade.watch: The funding-spread and bond-volatility rows above; the historical pivot was the central bank announcing a backstop facility.
s1_basis_trade.trap: In past episodes the 'safe' asset itself fell first - forced sellers sell what they can - so the flight-to-safety instinct lost money until the intervention.

s2_japan.mechanism: Surging Japanese yields pull decades of cheap yen funding home: the yen spikes on repatriation, and leveraged positions worldwide that were financed in yen get liquidated together - hitting high-momentum equities and emerging markets hardest.
benefits: Japanese banks and insurers as rates normalize
s2_japan.watch: The 30-year JGB row above (live official feed) and the yen; past unwinds announced themselves through the currency.
s2_japan.trap: Historical carry unwinds were violent but brief - the 2024 episode round-tripped within days; the durable shift was in Japanese financials, not the panic.

s3_private_credit.mechanism: One honest markdown forces everyone's marks: investor withdrawals hit gates, gated funds fire-sell into an illiquid market, and lending to mid-sized companies contracts just as they need to refinance.
bleeds: private-credit vehicles trading below stated asset value
benefits: holders of dry powder buying discounted credit afterwards
public high-quality credit as the flight destination
s3_private_credit.watch: The default-rate and redemption-gate rows above; public high-yield spreads are the honest proxy for hidden marks.
s3_private_credit.trap: Opacity means the repricing arrives as a sudden gap, not a trend - by the time it is public, the move has largely happened.

s4_dev_debt.mechanism: A cluster of sovereign defaults - not one - overwhelms the restructuring machinery: redemptions from emerging-market debt funds force indiscriminate selling of strong and weak credits alike, and stress spreads through common creditors.
benefits: and historically the buyers of defaulted debt after restructuring - among the best-documented recoveries in fixed income
s4_dev_debt.watch: The new-IMF-programs row above and the dollar's strength, which is usually the upstream cause.
s4_dev_debt.trap: Index diversification means one or two defaults barely register; the systemic wave this story warns of is exactly what official bailouts exist to prevent.

s5_china_deflation.mechanism: Deepening factory-gate deflation is exported as cheaper goods, compressing margins for competing producers everywhere - unless Beijing's stimulus response whipsaws the pressure into a sudden commodity and China-equity rebound.
benefits: long-term bonds in the deflation leg
Chinese equities and industrial metals in the stimulus leg
s5_china_deflation.watch: The producer-price row above and any stimulus announcement - the two legs point opposite directions.
s5_china_deflation.trap: Policy whipsaw: historically every stimulus rumor violently reversed the deflation trade within days.

s6_rare_earths.mechanism: Export restrictions tighten into denial: magnet and heavy-rare-earth supply to defense, vehicle, and robotics manufacturers halts, panic stockpiling begins, and processing capacity outside China re-rates from commodity business to strategic asset.
bleeds: vehicle and defense production schedules in the short run
s6_rare_earths.watch: The license-flow, blacklist, and ex-China premium rows above - the premium is the market's own severity gauge.
s6_rare_earths.trap: Historically these moves reversed as fast as they started on any truce headline, and diversified funds in the space often hold the Chinese producers too.

s7_stablecoins.mechanism: A run on a major stablecoin forces its reserves - tens of billions in short-term government debt - to liquidate within days, briefly dislocating the bill market while the crypto ecosystem's dollar rails seize and leveraged positions cascade.
benefits: historically the surviving issuer gained lasting market share after each depeg scare
s7_stablecoins.watch: The live peg-deviation and supply rows above (updated daily from the aggregator) - past runs announced themselves in the peg first.
s7_stablecoins.trap: Crypto markets have a long history of face-ripping rebounds inside downtrends; past episodes punished conviction in both directions.

s8_ai_capex.mechanism: The debt-financed buildout meets a revenue shortfall: one credit event at a leveraged data-center operator reprices all AI-adjacent borrowing, capital-spending guidance gets cut, chip orders fall, and power-demand forecasts deflate - the whole complex moves together because it was funded together.
bleeds: power producers priced on AI demand
benefits: and - the dot-com lesson - the post-bust survivors compounded for a decade
s8_ai_capex.watch: The capex-gap, revenue-gap, and refinancing rows above; credit stress historically led equity repricing.
s8_ai_capex.trap: Bubbles run longer than solvency: betting against this one early has been the era's classic ruin trade, which is why timing signals matter more than valuation.

s9_cre.mechanism: Office refinancing failures cluster into bank failures: deposit flight spreads to lookalike regional lenders, credit to small business contracts, and commercial-property marks finally reflect reality.
benefits: the largest banks via deposit inflows
and historically the whole sector rebounded within days of a backstop
s9_cre.watch: The bank-failure and office-delinquency rows above and the official problem-bank list.
s9_cre.trap: The 2023 backstop bottomed the sector in 48 hours - the policy response, not the failure, was the historical turning point.

s10_france.mechanism: Fiscal paralysis pushes French borrowing costs through crisis thresholds: banks holding the government's own bonds absorb the losses, the sovereign-bank doom loop reawakens, and stress spreads across euro-area borrowing costs.
bleeds: other high-debt euro members through contagion
benefits: and non-euro safe havens in every euro crisis
s10_france.watch: The OAT-Bund spread row above (live feed) - it is the market's single-number verdict on this story.
s10_france.trap: The central bank: euro-breakup positioning has been ruined repeatedly by ECB backstops built precisely for this scenario.

s11_consumer_debt.mechanism: Subprime stress spreads upward: rising late payments become charge-offs, lenders tighten, discretionary spending cracks, and the weakness travels from consumer lenders to retailers to the broad economy.
benefits: trade-down retailers in every past consumer squeeze
s11_consumer_debt.watch: The subprime-delinquency and BNPL rows above; the staples-versus-discretionary ratio is the market's own recession gauge.
s11_consumer_debt.trap: Lenders provision ahead of losses - their shares historically bottomed while delinquencies were still rising.

s12_gold_dedollar.mechanism: A reserve-weaponization event accelerates the slow shift: central banks swap dollar assets for gold at a faster pace, marginal foreign demand for government debt weakens, and the metal gains a structural, price-insensitive buyer.
bleeds: long-term government bonds via lost foreign demand
benefits: gold above all - the current central-bank buying era is the live example - plus non-dollar safe havens
s12_gold_dedollar.watch: The reserve-share row above (quarterly official data) and central-bank purchase reports.
s12_gold_dedollar.trap: This is measured in decades, not events - and gold miners have historically lagged the metal itself across full cycles.

s13_insurance.mechanism: A mega-catastrophe season collides with insurers already exiting exposed regions: property becomes uninsurable, collateral values fall, and the stress transmits to mortgages, regional lenders, and state backstops.
bleeds: property values and lenders in exposed regions
benefits: historically reinsurers AFTER the event as pricing hardened
and catastrophe-linked debt yields for risk-bearers
s13_insurance.watch: The insurer-exit and catastrophe-loss rows above plus the season's forecasts.
s13_insurance.trap: Positioning before the event absorbs the loss; the well-documented historical pattern favored the post-event hard market.

s14_pensions.mechanism: A rate spike forces leveraged pension strategies into collateral calls: they dump whatever is liquid, the selling pushes yields higher still, and the spiral continues until a central bank steps in - the UK lived this in 2022.
bleeds: long-term government bonds during the spiral itself
retirees' security in the slow version
benefits: whoever provided liquidity at the intervention - the 2022 central-bank entry marked the exact bottom - and retirement insurers structurally as rates rose
s14_pensions.watch: The funded-ratio row above (live monthly feed) and long-bond volatility.
s14_pensions.trap: Identical to the basis trade: buying the falling 'safe' asset before the intervention caught knives for days.

s15_ai_power.mechanism: Data-center demand outruns the grid so badly that curtailments, connection queues, and building moratoria stall the buildout - rising household bills turn it political, and the constraint moves from engineering to consent.
bleeds: utilities caught between regulators and demand
benefits: and nuclear/gas capacity - though see the trap
s15_ai_power.watch: The interconnection-wait and moratoria rows above and capacity-auction prices.
s15_ai_power.trap: The famous version of this trade assumes the buildout CONTINUES; this story's actual blow-up - moratoria stopping it - points the opposite way for the same names.

s16_copper.mechanism: A structural deficit meets a supply shock - a major mine closure removes years of planned supply - and the metal prices high enough to ration demand, raising costs for every grid, vehicle, and data-center project simultaneously.
benefits: producing miners with volume to sell
s16_copper.watch: The mine-disruption and deficit rows above and exchange inventory levels.
s16_copper.trap: The political risk that causes the shocks sits inside the producers themselves - the closed mine may be the one you were counting on.

s17_water.mechanism: Severe drought hits a chip hub, a farm belt, and cooling-dependent power at once: an unpriced input becomes a binding constraint, cutting industrial output regionally and feeding into food prices.
benefits: historically crop prices in drought years
s17_water.watch: The reservoir and drought rows above (live official feed for the largest US reservoir).
s17_water.trap: There is no pure play - broad 'water' funds are mostly global industrials, while the shock is local; the honest effects are second-order.

s18_food_fertilizer.mechanism: Fertilizer export restrictions cut application in poorer countries, next season's yields fall, grain prices spike, and food inflation becomes social and fiscal stress in import-dependent nations - looping back into the developing-world debt story.
benefits: fertilizer producers in every past squeeze
s18_food_fertilizer.watch: The FAO food-price row above (live feed) and the export-curb indicator.
s18_food_fertilizer.trap: Fertilizer stress historically reversed violently when curbs lifted, taking back most of the move.

s19_lithography.mechanism: Conflict or blockade around Taiwan stops the fabs that make nearly all leading-edge chips: every electronics supply chain seizes within a quarter, and the shock is large enough that markets themselves may not function normally.
bleeds: and anything with a chip in it
s19_lithography.watch: The tension and export-control rows above; false-alarm cycles have historically outnumbered real escalations many times over.
s19_lithography.trap: In the true scenario, settlement and market access are themselves at risk - analysis that assumes functioning markets may not apply.

s20_sea_lanes.mechanism: A chokepoint closes - this board just watched Hormuz do it - and shipping rates, war-risk insurance, and energy prices spike together while longer reroutes quietly shrink effective global capacity; cable cuts do the same for data.
s20_sea_lanes.watch: The live strait-transit feed and cable-incident rows above.
s20_sea_lanes.trap: This board's own history shows it: reopening headlines crushed the shipping move within days - persistence of the disruption was everything.

s21_clearinghouses.mechanism: A major member defaults into a volatile market and the clearinghouse's loss waterfall activates: surviving members face assessments and de-risk simultaneously, margin requirements spiral procyclically, and the plumbing everyone assumed away becomes the crisis itself.
benefits: almost nothing leveraged - which is the honest answer; cash
and physical assets have no counterparty
s21_clearinghouses.watch: The clearing-mandate rollout row above and any clearinghouse margin announcements.
s21_clearinghouses.trap: The deepest on the board: in a true clearing failure, a winning derivative position may itself not pay out.

context.intro: The famous dials, for contrast. These are the most-watched macro gauges in the world - shown here so you can compare them with this tracker's structural lens. They are not part of the score. When they disagree with the gauge above, that divergence is the story: markets price these continuously, while the risks this tracker follows are the kind markets historically ignored until they ruptured.

items.label: VIX
items.note: Expected US stock-market volatility - the most-watched fear gauge. Calm markets usually sit below ~20.

items.label: 10y-2y curve
items.note: 10-year minus 2-year Treasury yield. A negative (inverted) reading has historically preceded US recessions - with long and variable lags.

items.label: High-yield spread
items.note: The extra yield markets demand to lend to risky companies - the market's own price of credit stress. Calm is roughly below ~4.

items.label: Chicago Fed NFCI
items.note: The Chicago Fed's broad financial-conditions index across money, debt, and equity markets. Negative = looser (calmer) than average.

items.label: Unemployment
items.note: The US unemployment rate - the classic real-economy dial, updated monthly.
